core: the lesson is a bridge from design craft to the business half of product work
products are built by organizations with budgets, timelines, and goals
design as a business activity: one discipline among several inside an organization
the value of design in general terms: adoption, efficiency, and satisfaction (no ROI formulas)
design work happens inside budgets and business decisions
the curriculum map: introduction-to-business, accounting, and finance come next and own the depth
the honest framing: design literacy and business literacy are two halves of the same work
supporting: NN/g's working definition of UX: all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services, and its products
usability as part of the UX umbrella, measured via success rates and customer satisfaction
organizations convert inputs (resources, materials, human resources, capital) into products and services on schedules and budgets
what introduction to business covers: the nature of business and organizations

accounting concepts (ledgers, statements) and finance concepts (valuation, investment analysis)

claims.claim: Nielsen Norman Group defines user experience as encompassing all aspects of the end-user's interaction with the company, its services, and its products, and notes that high-quality UX requires a seamless merging of disciplines including engineering, marketing, graphical and industrial design, and interface design.

NN/g describes usability as a quality attribute defined by five components — learnability, efficiency, memorability, errors, and satisfaction — where efficiency is how quickly users can perform tasks and satisfaction is how pleasant the design is to use.

NN/g states that on the web, usability is a necessary condition for survival — if a website is difficult to use, people leave — and that for internal products usability is a matter of employee productivity.

Digital.gov (U.S. General Services Administration) describes usability as how easily and effectively people accomplish their goals using a product, measured through usability testing with success rates and customer satisfaction, and places usability as one part of the larger user experience (UX) umbrella.

OpenStax Introduction to Business states that production turns inputs such as natural resources, raw materials, human resources, and capital into outputs — the products and services customers receive — and illustrates the process with a road-bridge project delivered on a tight schedule and specific budget.
OpenStax Introduction to Business defines a business as an organization that strives for a profit by providing goods and services desired by its customers.
The value of good design can be stated in general terms — it affects adoption, efficiency, and satisfaction — and this lesson deliberately avoids ROI formulas, percentages, and dollar figures.

The curriculum map: the Part III subjects that follow this bridge lesson are introduction-to-business, accounting, and finance, and they own the business and money depth; introduction to business covers what a business is and how organizations create goods and services.

Design decisions are also business decisions because design work costs money and time inside an organization's budget and timeline; designers bring evidence about user behavior, errors, and satisfaction to those trade-off conversations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Specific quantitative claims about design's financial payoff vary by context and method; NN/g publishes rule-of-thumb estimates (such as a usability budget of about 10% roughly doubling quality metrics) while industry caution holds that ROI-style numbers differ across industries, products, and measures.
positions: NN/g's Usability 101 article offers rule-of-thumb estimates for usability spending and outcomes
Practitioners caution that ROI-style figures are context-dependent and contested
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson states only general, sourced value claims (adoption, efficiency, satisfaction) and explicitly defers all quantification to the accounting and finance subjects; no ROI figures are published here.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Usability.gov's content now redirects to Digital.gov, and the legacy usability.gov pages describe business benefits in different terms than the current Digital.gov topic page.
positions: Legacy usability.gov pages list benefits such as reduced development costs and increased sales
The current Digital.gov topic page frames usability through goals, success rates, and customer satisfaction
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only the current Digital.gov topic page (registered as digitalgov-usability) and does not repeat legacy benefit lists.
